Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Clara Mendoza had not expected the abandoned storage facility on the edge of town to become a cage. When the heavy metal door clicked shut and the bolt slid home, she was certain she would soon be released. Instead, the space offered no exits, only a single barred window and a concrete floor that forced her to sit with her shoulders hunched forward. For days, her neck ached from the rigid angle, a sharp, unyielding tension that never eased. The captor controlled every movement; there was no negotiation, no alternative route out, only the crushing weight of having no options. When she was finally freed, the physical ache in her neck lingered, but the true shift was quieter. She returned to her suburban home, but the safety she had always assumed was a given suddenly felt like a fragile illusion. In the weeks that followed, Clara found herself rewinding the event in her head, searching for a miscalculation she might have made. She told herself the ordeal was overblown, that it did not define her reality, yet the thoughts would not stop. She would sit at her kitchen table, tracing the same sequence of moments, wondering if a different word, a different posture, might have changed the outcome. At her job as a project manager, she coordinated cross-functional teams and tight deadlines. When a supplier pulled out of a contract and the department’s locked supply closet sealed shut during a routine inventory audit, her breath caught. The walls felt too close. She stepped back from the doorway, telling herself she was simply tired, but her pulse hammered against the familiar ache in her neck. She could not stay in that room. She walked out, avoided the facility’s lower floors, and stopped taking the elevator to the executive suites. Her weeks settled into a quiet pattern. She stopped inviting former colleagues over. She could not explain why she refused the small linen closet in the hallway, or why she chose conference rooms with glass walls and double doors propped open. At home, her shoulders never truly dropped. She checked the locks three times before bed, listening for footsteps on the porch, startled when the garbage truck rumbled down the street. She was aware she was safe, yet her body answered to a different clock. She reacted to the slamming of a cupboard as if a door were being forced open. The exhaustion was absolute. She used to laugh at dinner parties, used to plan vacations months ahead, but now she felt hollowed out, as if someone had carefully emptied her. The world felt inherently unpredictable; you could never know who might cross the line, what moment might trap you. Six months after the facility incident, Clara finally sat in a therapist’s office. The waitroom’s partitioned chairs, the soft hum of the HVAC system, the way the receptionist’s keys clinked in a locked drawer—all of it made her chest tighten. She had come to believe she was broken, that the person she once was had been replaced by someone who flinched at shadows. What frightened her most was not the past itself, but the certainty that it was happening again, that the locks were still engaged, that the road ahead offered no alternatives. She wanted to sleep without bracing her neck, wanted to open a door and feel only air instead of consequence. She hoped, for the first time in a long time, to find a way out of the room she could no longer see herself leaving.
